prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Here take my picture; though I bid farewell Thine, in my heart, where my soul dwells, shall dwell. 'Tis like me now, but I dead, 'twill be more When we are shadows both, than 'twas before. When weather-beaten I come back, my hand Perhaps with rude oars torn, or sun beams tann'd, My face and breast of haircloth, and my head With care's rash sudden storms being o'erspread, My body'a sack of bones, broken within, And powder's blue stains scatter'd on my skin; If rival fools tax thee to'have lov'd a man So foul and coarse as, oh, I may seem then, This shall say what I was, and thou shalt say, "Do his hurts reach me? doth my worth decay? Or do they reach his judging mind, that he Should now love less, what he did love to see? That which in him was fair and delicate, Was but the milk which in love's childish state Did nurse it; who now is grown strong enough To feed on that, which to disus'd tastes seems tough."

### Option 1: Elegant & Professional Modern Prose (Recommended)
> "Please accept this portrait as I bid you farewell; though I depart, your image remains forever enshrined within my heart, the very home of my soul. While this likeness resembles me today, it will prove even truer when I am gone and we both have become mere shadows. 
> 
> Should I return weathered by adversity—my hands torn by oars or darkened by the sun, my body worn and frail, my spirit burdened by life’s sudden storms, and my skin marked by the stains of powder—foolish rivals may mock you for having loved a man who appears so rough and altered.

> If so, let this portrait bear witness to who I was, and reply to them: *'Do his physical scars diminish my worth? Do they impair his judgment, causing him to love me any less? The delicate beauty of youth was merely the milk that sustained our love in its infancy. Now mature and resilient, our love is strong enough to feed on life’s harsher realities—sustenance that weaker, unaccustomed hearts would find too bitter to endure.'*"

### Option 2: Polished & Modernized Verse (Maintaining Poetic Structure)
> Take this, my portrait, as I bid farewell;  
> Within my heart, where dwells my soul, you dwell.  
> 'Tis like me now, but when I am no more,  
> 'Twill bear my truer likeness than before.  
> 
> When weather-beaten I return at last—  
> My hands by heavy oars or sun overcast,  
> My brow by sudden storms of care oppressed,  
> A sack of bones, with powder on my chest—  
> 
> If foolish rivals mock that you could care

> *To nurse its youth when bound in softest silk;*  
> *Now grown mature, our love has grown so tough*  
> *To feed on strength, though lesser tastes find rough."*

Please accept this portrait as I depart; though I am leaving, your image remains permanently fixed within my deepest soul. Although this painting captures my current appearance, it will represent me even better in the future when we have both passed away and become mere spirits. 

Upon my return, worn down by harsh elements, my hands might be calloused and torn from rowing oars or darkened by intense sunlight. My skin will feel as rough as coarse fabric, my head prematurely aged by sudden bouts of intense stress, my frame reduced to an internally shattered bag of bones, and my skin marked with blue gunpowder burns. 

Should foolish suitors mock you for having loved a man who appears so ruined and unappealing, this painting will testify to who I used to be. You can then challenge them by asking: "Do his physical injuries diminish my worth? Have his battle scars corrupted his intellect, making him care any less for my beauty than he once did?" 

My former handsome, delicate appearance was merely like milk that nourished our love during its infancy. Now that our affection has fully matured, it is strong enough to consume rugged hardships that would seem unpalatable to those with weak or unrefined tastes.
outputs.L3:
Here is an expanded, well-structured text based on the bullet points, written in an eloquent, reflective tone:

***

As the hour of departure arrives and fate demands our temporary separation, I place into your hands a final token of my affection: my portrait. While this painted likeness remains behind to keep you company, it represents only a fraction of the exchange between us. For though I leave my painted self in your care, I depart carrying your image indelibly engraved upon my heart—a sacred impression that no distance, duration, or hardship can ever erase.

There is a quiet, melancholic truth to this gift. Today, the canvas may seem a pale, static imitation of my warm blood and vitality. Yet, I reflect that with the passage of time, the picture will become an even truer representation of me. When our mortal years have run their course and we both inevitably transition into shadows, this unaging portrait will remain as the truest testament to the living man I once was, bridging the gap between life and the beyond.

I hold no illusions about the toll the coming days will take. I fully expect to return from this journey physically transformed—battered by harsh elements, bearing the deep scars of battle, and aged prematurely by unrelenting trial. The smooth countenance and youthful vigor captured on this canvas will soon be surrendered to the cruel realities of conflict and distance. 

Should I return a physically ruined man, this portrait will serve a practical purpose. There will inevitably be rivals and skeptics who criticize your devotion, mocking you for remaining bound to a weathered, broken shell. In those moments, this image will stand as silent evidence of my former self, vindicating your choice and proving to the world that your beloved was once whole, handsome, and worthy of your grace.

Ultimately, however, our bond does not rely on a painted past to justify itself. While shallow, youthful attraction depends entirely on superficial beauty and fleeting charms, true and mature love operates on a far deeper plane. Love that has grown resilient through shared devotion is impervious to physical decay. Though the world may see only my scars and worn frame upon my return, I take comfort in knowing that our love is strong enough to look past the ruin of the body, enduring long after youth has faded.
outputs.L4:
The shadow of a long and perilous journey now falls across my path—a voyage through unforgiving lands and treacherous seas that promises to exact a heavy toll upon the flesh. I know the thief that travel is: it steals the smoothness from the skin, the brightness from the eyes, and the vigor from the posture, leaving in their place the hollowed cheeks, graying locks, and weathered lines of severe physical deterioration. Fearing that the cruel machinery of time and hardship will return me to you a broken remnant of the man who now departs, I place into your hands this portrait. It is a carefully rendered likeness of my present self, painted while my youth remains unmarred and my countenance intact. 

Consider this canvas not a monument to my vanity, but a fortress built for your protection and mine. Should I return bearing the disfiguring scars of my travels, reduced to a ghost of my former vigor, the world will undoubtedly offer its sharp scorns and pitiless mockery. They will laugh at the ruin of what was once fair. In those moments of public cruelty or private doubt, I bid you hold this portrait up against my shattered frame. Let it serve as your defense—a proof to all who gaze upon my decrepitude that I was not always a wreck of nature, and that the man you chose was once worthy of the eyes’ delight. 

Yet, beneath this practical shield lies a far deeper truth about the nature of our bond. In its earliest days, our affection fed upon the simple, visible graces of the body: the symmetry of features, the flush of health, the fleeting charm of youthful form. Beauty is indeed the milk that nurses love in its tender infancy; it inspires the first sighs and kindles the initial spark. But a love that remains reliant on superficial perfection is destined to starve as the flesh decays. 

By offering you this image before I am ruined by the road, we acknowledge that our devotion has outgrown its cradling stages. The painting captures the mortal shell, but our bond has migrated to a higher kingdom. Our love has reached its full maturity, hardening into something indestructible that no longer requires the sweet poison of physical perfection to sustain itself. 

Take this portrait, then, and keep it near. If the road breaks my body and steals my grace, let the painted wood preserve the memory of my youth for the superficial world to judge. But between the two of us, let it be a monument to a far greater miracle: that while my image on canvas remains frozen in time, the soul that loves you will return to you weathered and altered, yet tied to yours by a spiritual devotion that physical decay can never touch.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a 17th-century metaphysical poem in heroic couplets where a speaker leaves a portrait with their beloved before going on a harsh voyage, reflecting on how physical beauty fades but true love matures.
counterfactuals.output:
Before I tempt the wild and salt-blown sea,
Accept this quiet shadow, love, of me;
Where painted youth, in motionless arrest,
Sits locked within the limner’s velvet chest.
My living flesh must sail where tempests blow,
To freeze in northern ice, or burn below;
The biting frost shall plow upon my cheek,
And rust the vigor that thy kisses seek;
The sun will scorch, the winter gale will strip
The fleeting vermeil from this parting lip.

Yet this small picture knows no ocean-gale,
Nor shall its blushing colors faint or fail;
It holds the quiet of a summer day,
Unmarred by bitter brine or slow decay.
When tempests render all my features grim,
And steal the vigor from each weary limb,
Weep not, my Saint, to see the canvas mock
The battered sailor tossed upon the rock.

For outward grace is but a fleeting spark,
A sublunary phantom in the dark,
Mere dross and clay that time and tides erode,
To leave the soul a purified abode.
Love is no slave to skin, nor ruled by eye,
That with the withered cheek must faint and die;
As gold is prov’d within the furnace blast,
So rougher seas shall make my love outlast.

Then keep the shade to show what time erased,
And keep the heart, which thy own virtue graced:
Though stormy waves this mortal frame subdue,
Age mars the flesh, but love matures for you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

**To His Lady, Upon Presenting His Portrait Before Travel**

The tide now calls, the restless canvas swells,
And cruel wind commands my swift depart;
Yet ere I leave the realm where beauty dwells,
I place my shadow near thy constant heart.

’Tis but the labor of a limner’s hand,
In silent pigment on a panel laid;
A frozen ghost to watch the lonely land,
While I am tossed where surging waves are made.

Yet take this counterfeit, my noble dear,
When leagues stretch wide between my love and thee;
Though wood and paint can shed no parting tear,
These painted eyes shall never turn from thee.

For as the sun leaves shadow on the dial,
To mark the hours until his light return,
So let this image wait upon thy smile,
And keep the lamp of our devotion burn.

My mortal frame to foreign shores must roam,
By treacherous winds and fickle fortune led;
Yet in thy breast my spirit finds its home—
Look on this face, and know I am not dead. 

Until the sea shall yield me back again,
Let this poor shade my solemn vow renew:
Art holds my form through peril, storm, and pain,
But living grace and soul remain with you.

counterfactuals.prompt: What is the poem that begins with "Here take my picture; though I bid farewell"?
counterfactuals.output:
The poem that begins with that line is **"Elegy V: His Picture"** (sometimes simply titled **"His Picture"**) by the English Metaphysical poet **John Donne**.

Here is the full text of the poem:

> Here take my picture; though I bid farewell,
> Thine eye shall be in the same aspect still,
> 'Tis like I shall be alter'd in the goings,
> With care and business, warmth by travel's blowings,
> Riding, and heat, leave this skin weather-beaten,
> My body's a sack of bones, broken and eaten,
> My hair and beard grown white, my eyes grown dim,
> Such altered stuff, sir, shall I come to him.
> 
> Shadow, that matches not the body's size,
> Doth look like that, which it doth represent:
> So this shadow, which thy memory supplies,
> Will keep the form of what it once was meant.
> 
> Take then this picture, though it be no more
> Than a dull shadow of what I was before;
> And when weather-beaten I return again,
> If thy love remain, mine shall not be in vain.
> If rival love should make thee change thy mind,
> Look on this picture, and there read how kind,
> How constant I was when I gave it thee;
> And let it speak when I am far away. 

*(Note: Variations in spelling and lineation exist across different historical editions of Donne's works.)*

### Context
In this poem, the speaker gives his portrait to his lover before departing on a long and potentially hazardous journey. He acknowledges that physical travel, age, and hardship will change his body, but the picture will remain a constant reminder of his youthful love and devotion.
